title: Is anyone actually building games with open-source models instead of Claude or Codex?
author: Gaebabi
selftext:
I'm curious if anyone here is building games using open-source models instead of Claude or Codex.

If you are, I'd love to see what you've built!

I'm especially interested in how well these models handle large, complex game projects. Can they consistently follow instructions and make meaningful changes to an existing codebase without going off track?

Also, is anyone running open models through Codex, OpenCode, or a similar agent harness? I'd love to hear what models and setups you're using.

In my experience, GPT-6.1 Sol is pretty much the only model I've tried that consistently understands what I'm asking on the first try and actually does what I intended. Though to be fair, I tend to give pretty vague instructions sometimes, lol.

I'd really like to know if anyone has had better results with open models, especially on larger Unity or Unreal projects.

Feel free to share your projects, workflows, or even your failures. I'm genuinely curious how far open models have come.

comments.author: aura-32
comments.body:
A related angle that might interest you: open models inside the game at runtime, not just for writing the code. I'm the dev of Hatched, a browser city sim where every resident is an AI, and we decided early not to lock it to one provider. Players can bring their own key for Anthropic, OpenRouter, or any OpenAI-compatible API, which is the format most self-hosted model servers speak. By default the citizens actually run on a free local rules brain, and autopilot only calls a model for the moments that matter, like a job offer or a fight.

That split is what makes swapping models workable, because a weaker model only has to handle a few short, well-scoped decisions instead of the whole game. I suspect the same applies to coding: an open model that drifts on "refactor my Unity project" can do fine when it's given one small, well-defined change at a time with a clear spec.

replies.author: Gaebabi
replies.body: That's a really interesting perspective. I think I was looking at this too narrowly. From my experience, open models should handle those kinds of tasks just fine. Thanks for sharing!

replies.author: Own_Badger6076
replies.body: i mean you would never want to lock it into a cloud provider anyway, that's a fast way to cost yourself a lot of money. Local is the way to go so long as you can use a custom made one that's small enough to do exactly what you want without requiring heavy hardware.

replies.author: Gaebabi
replies.body:
Yeah, I've definitely felt that too. I've tried quite a few approaches, but I just couldn't get the speed and performance I wanted, which is why I made this post.

Honestly, frontier models have gotten incredibly good lately. My biggest disappointment was getting the chance to experiment with two A100 80GB GPUs at work, with API costs covered as well. I tried Qwen 3.8 and DeepSeek V4, but both were pretty disappointing for my use case. They honestly felt worse than Terra 6.1.

replies.author: Gaebabi
replies.body: I've had a similar experience with Qwen needing more hand-holding. Does prompt processing get painfully slow with longer contexts?

replies.author: throwaway275275275
replies.body: I never let it get longer than 128k if I can help it, which is part of the handholding, having to start every task in a fresh session and having the tasks small enough that they fit in the context

comments.author: No_Dig_7017
comments.body: Yes. For the curiosity and learning mostly. It definitely takes more manual work. I'm using Deepseek 4.1 Flash 1017 iq2_xs self hosted on my rig. It gets confused with very long prompts, sometimes loses instructions along the way and says he's done with a task when he's not, which causes several iterations. That said I have no limit to what I can ask him. I literally leave it working overnight and come back to progress in the morning. I'd say it's still too early but there's some things you can achieve if you're interested. For actual professional use, I think it's better to go cloud for now. My next experiment will probably be non flash deepseek in Opencode Go

replies.author: No_Dig_7017
replies.body: Another thing I heard works very well is using a cloud model for orchestration/validation and a local model for the brunt of the implementation but I haven't tried it yet

replies.author: Gaebabi
replies.body: That's smth I've been wanting to try too!

replies.author: Gaebabi
replies.body: That's pretty much what I've experienced too, especially the part about claiming tasks are done when they're not, haha. I'm curious about your overnight runs though. How much useful work does it actually get done without your intervention?

replies.author: No_Dig_7017
replies.body: It's difficult to say, I'm decompiling an old dos game to enhance it so he's got to mostly copy a reference. Usually he advances the amount of things we can do in the game but they are all buggy and missing parts. Then I go in in the morning give him a list of corrections to make and we iterate. Some he resolves but some I've been stuck on for days. When I fully guide him focusing on a single feature at a time he usually gets it though.
